title: Bonebrake v. Cox
lead: After a fire destroyed their bowling equipment, the Coxes hired a dealer to supply and install replacements before league play. The dealer died with machines defective and work incomplete, and the buyers’ effort to finish the job became the basis of an adverse price judgment that the court of appeals reversed.

actors.name: Donald and Claude Cox
actors.role: Owners rebuilding Tamarack Bowl in Missouri Valley, Iowa.

actors.name: Woodrow Simek
actors.role: Nebraska sole proprietor who sold and installed bowling equipment.

actors.name: Frances Bonebrake
actors.role: Simek’s sister and administratrix pursuing the unpaid price.

actors.name: Judge Talbot Smith
actors.role: Visiting judge who authored the Eighth Circuit opinion.

proceedings: A special master rejected the buyers’ counterclaims and recommended the unpaid price less a credit; the district court entered $27,000 for the estate. The Eighth Circuit reversed and remanded on accepted-goods remedies, Article 2 coverage, and anticipatory repudiation.
limits: The court did not calculate a substitute recovery or make every seller’s death repudiation. The narrative’s $20,000 and $7,000 payments differ from the reproduced lawyer letter’s $27,500 total; no reconciliation is invented. The decision applies Iowa law in 1974.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A fire leads to two equipment-and-installation contracts
sections.cue: What did Simek undertake to supply?
paragraphs: Donald and Claude Cox had operated Tamarack Bowl in Missouri Valley, Iowa, for about twenty years when a February 5, 1968 fire destroyed its equipment. They decided to rebuild and contracted with Woodrow Simek, a Nebraska bowling-alley operator and equipment dealer working as a sole proprietor.

On April 17, the Coxes agreed to pay $20,000 for used lane beds, ball returns, chairs and seating, a ball-cleaning machine, lockers, balls, racks, rental shoes, radarays, and foundation materials, delivered and installed. Simek would resurface and finish the lanes and warranted workmanship, materials, and compliance with American Bowling Congress specifications. Payments tracked signing, commencement of foundation work, and completed installation.

Simek hired Ilert Avery, known as Blackie, for most installation. The unfinished building delayed lane work until August. On August 23, a second agreement called for ten used Brunswick Model A pinspotters, installed, for $35,000, with a one-year guarantee of motors and gearboxes. Neither agreement set a completion date. But league play ordinarily began in late August or early September for four rounds over thirty-six weeks, and delay risked losing a round. League members volunteered to help open the alley.

sections.title: Defective machines and the seller’s death leave no workable completion plan
sections.cue: Why did the buyers take over?
paragraphs: By September 4, the pinspotters stood at the lanes, but the special master later found them inoperative, in poor condition, and not installed as promised. Most needed work on frozen bearings and replacement parts. The Coxes and volunteers dismantled and repaired them with Blackie’s advice. He knew of their dissatisfaction, but Simek died September 6 before they could speak directly with him.

The judicial narrative reports $20,000 paid toward pinspotters and $7,000 toward the April agreement. Several April items were missing; delivered ball returns and radarays remained uninstalled. The buyers searched Simek’s warehouses and contacted suppliers, Blackie, and Simek’s sister, Frances Bonebrake. They found little usable equipment and nobody able to organize performance.

Only after those efforts failed did they order missing items themselves. An altercation around September 12 prompted Blackie to leave, and specialists finished repair and installation. Counsel’s September 17 letter described unfinished installation, repairs, expected lost income, and records kept to substantiate a loss claim. Bonebrake denied receipt, but the master found no reason to believe the letter had not been mailed. The alley opened October 14, allowing only three league rounds.

sections.title: The estate obtains a price judgment despite the defects
sections.cue: What errors did the appellate court review?
paragraphs: As administratrix, Bonebrake sought the unpaid contract price. The Coxes counterclaimed for losses and argued that Simek or the estate breached first. The special master rejected both positions and recommended $28,000 unpaid price minus $1,000 for the seller’s value of unaccepted goods. The district court entered $27,000 for the estate.

The master recognized the harshness of requiring payment for seriously defective pinspotters but believed the Uniform Commercial Code demanded it. He also excluded the April mixed goods-and-services agreement from Article 2 and treated the buyers’ takeover as their breach. Although he did not expressly resolve anticipatory repudiation, that conclusion implicitly rejected it.

Iowa law governed under an unchallenged ruling. Judge Talbot Smith, sitting by designation from the Eastern District of Michigan, wrote for the Eighth Circuit panel with Judges Heaney and Stephenson. The panel examined notice and cure, Article 2 coverage, and that implied rejection of repudiation under commercially practical Code principles.

sections.title: Acceptance preserves a damages remedy under a different notice rule
sections.cue: Why was the September letter sufficient?
paragraphs: The master found that installation required making the pinspotters operative, constituting a fitness warranty the equipment did not meet. But he believed inadequate notice and interference with cure eliminated the buyers’ warranty remedies.

Iowa §554.2607(3)(a), corresponding to Uniform Commercial Code §2-607(3)(a), governed accepted goods. It required notice of breach within a reasonable time after discovery. That notice need not list every defect, claim damages, or threaten suit. It must convey that the transaction was troublesome and claimed to involve breach, permitting negotiation.

The master instead imported the more particularized rule for rejection in §554.2605(1), addressing omitted discoverable defects when cure was possible or in specified merchant dealings. The September 17 letter readily satisfied the accepted-goods rule: it identified needed repairs, failure of the guarantee, incomplete installation, and recorded loss expenditures. The estate’s argument that no heightened specificity had actually been demanded did not persuade the panel.

The cure analysis made the same category error. Section 554.2508 concerned a rejected nonconforming tender. These buyers accepted goods and sought damages; accepting a later cure proposal was not a prerequisite to all recovery. Refusing it could affect mitigation and damages, but did not erase the warranty claim.

sections.title: The April agreement predominantly supplied goods
sections.cue: Why did installation not remove it from Article 2?
paragraphs: The master relied on substantial labor, a lump price, and indivisibility to exclude the April contract. But Article 2 covered transactions in goods, defined by movability when identified to the contract. This was tangible, portable commercial equipment, and the agreement itself described equipment, workmanship and materials, and a purchase price.

Later attachment did not turn the bargain into house construction. The lane beds arrived in three prefabricated sections, joined and screwed to a wooden foundation on concrete. They were used goods already removed from an earlier installation, which plainly had not made them permanently immovable.

The panel compared decisions about electrified flooring, poured concrete with labor, and an automobile dealership where services furthered a goods transaction. It distinguished an agreement expressly selling data analysis and reporting, and declined to develop blood-transfusion or cosmetics analogies with different facts and policies.

The governing predominant-factor inquiry asked whether the transaction primarily supplied services with incidental goods or goods with incidental labor. An artist’s painting contract illustrated the former, and installation of a bathroom water heater the latter. The Coxes chiefly purchased replacements for burned bowling equipment. Installation did not change that central purpose, so Article 2 covered the April agreement.

sections.title: The full circumstances justified protective action before performance ended
sections.cue: Why was the estate’s later offer too late?
paragraphs: The court did not equate every seller’s death with repudiation. Here the sole proprietorship, severe defects, absent equipment, approaching league schedule, fruitless searches, and lack of anybody able to continue performance together indicated rejection of the continuing obligation. The Coxes initially tried to carry out the bargain and purchased replacements only after those efforts failed. Whether Bonebrake met them once or twice did not matter because she could offer no productive course.

Under §554.2610 and the Code commentary, repudiation did not require literal impossibility or malevolence. Conduct reasonably indicating rejection sufficed even while the performance period remained open. The panel found clear error in the implied contrary finding and regarded the buyers’ protective steps as justified rather than a prior breach.

Administrators arriving September 17 lacked relevant business experience and did not know what remained necessary. Even if their later completion proposal counted as retraction under §554.2611, the buyers had already materially changed position, making it too late.

sections.title: The estate’s judgment is reversed without a substitute damages calculation
sections.cue: What remained for the trial court?
paragraphs: On July 2, 1974, the Eighth Circuit reversed the $27,000 judgment and remanded for proceedings consistent with its rulings. Both agreements received the proper goods-law analysis, acceptance no longer barred warranty damages through misplaced rejection rules, and the buyers’ response to repudiation was not treated as their breach.
The Court did not calculate the buyers’ recovery or enter a replacement monetary judgment. Mitigation and the support for particular losses remained relevant. No separate opinion was issued.
